attributes.Content:
As an artist I am balancing the personal with the social. Although I take my own experiences as the starting point for my work, I reflect on my own concern through the behavior and perspectives of others. I research factors that determine who I am – cultural heritage, national identity, the changes I experienced migrating to the Netherlands, social networks and connections – and translate them to
larger socio-cultural themes.
By enlarging upon these metaphors for my own life I am able to grasp larger subject matters. I try to make the personal impersonal, but while doing so I realize I am showing more of myself than I ever expected to. I started to use my own experience as the basis for my art after moving to Amsterdam in 2001 to study at the Rietveld Academy. I realized how much my life had altered by migrating to a different country. It occurred to me that my daily rhythm was no longer the same, my eating habits changed and my social life changed drastically after I had moved away from my family, friends and familiar life in Tel Aviv. I also used the distance from my country of origin to reflect upon former life in Israel.
My early projects I Want to be Green (2005)and Rijtjeshuizen (2006-2008), for example, I documented the experiences of migrants. I shared the stories of Israeli migrants in the Netherlands, and Dutch migrants in Israel in video works and sculptures . Both were exhibited at the Joods Historisch Museum in Amsterdam.
 I continued this research-based approach for my 2011 project, Chief of Stuff, a mixed media installation work that explored the power dynamics in the Israeli army through the principles of the ideological warrior: loyalty, sacrifice, obedience and faith in tradition. As a young man, I was part of a prestigious combat unit, having the ambitions to serve my country. But, as a more mature artist, I distanced myself from this time. With Chief of Stuff I reflect upon a feeling of alienation. Who had I been then? What were the forces that made me that person? In a series of work I endlessly reproduce my self-portrait using the cliched symbols of the military might: the enemy as a target; the fallen
soldier as an angel, the western fighter image with the figure of the Japanese Samurai.
In my 2011 project The Chief of Staff, a continuation of Chief of Stuff, I made a site-specific installation for a Herzliya Museum of Contemporary Art in IsraelI decided to focus on the structure of Israeli military command. Through interviews with military historians and experts, I was able to portray the Israeli military command personnel hierarchy, which I then captured in 161 unique paintings of each rank in the hierarchy, representing each military commander as a fallen angel.
These projects both stemmed from my own experience, but do not represent who I am; my role in them was that of social commentator, although the imagery was surreal or abstract.
This changed when I began working on Food Chain Project in 2008. For this project I embarked on a
very personal journey. Realizing how much my eating habits had changed after moving to the
Netherlands, I decided to write down every single thing that I ate and drank for an entire year,
banning myself from looking at the list until the year was over.
In 2013 I started to translate all the gathered data into sculptures, representing all the produce and
 products I consumed, which I then presented in one single supermarket-like installation. I created
 
thousands of sculptures in stark white plaster, making molds of actual food items. Four years later, I
 made a second installation of Food Chain Project for the newly opened LAM. This time I created the
 works in porcelain, and presented them on a clean shelving system. I tested my own technical skills,
 working in a delicate and costly medium.
 Thinking about my personal consumption habits, I started to research the social implications of
 individual consumption choices on global food issues. By presenting all the 8,000 products I
 consumed in a year, I aimed to raise awareness and generate a wider discussion on global food issues.
 The project highlights overconsumption, while hundreds of millions of people around the world still
 suffer from hunger every day.
 Presenting the work in its totality however made me realize how personal this project was. It was the
 vast number of bottles of wine that I consumed. It were the hamburgers that I ate. Rather than just
 presenting the 8,000 objects, it felt like I presented myself. If you are what you eat, as the saying
 goes, I realized the installation was a large scale self-portrait.
 Food Chain Project also sparked my interest in the history and meaning of the self-portrait. In a time
 that selfies and portraits are made in an instant I address the need of self-exploration and personal
 development. Psychologist Terri Apter argues that taking selfies is all about people trying to figure
 out who they are and projecting this to other people. “It’s a kind of self-definition. We all like the idea
 of being sort of in control of our image and getting attention, being noticed, being part of the culture.”
 I realized that self-definition and self-exploration are far from new. According to media psychology
 expert Pamela B. Rutledge, Ph.D. humans have long demonstrated an interest in both. From the early
 Greeks to present day, people have used self-study and self-observation to explore identity and
 sense of self. “Trying to figure out who we are and what we’re about is a distinctly human pursuit for
 almost everyone, whether you are trying to find greater consciousness or figure out what moved you
 to buy the blue shoes.”
 In my research into the self-portrait I realized that instead of presenting and representing
 metaphors, I wanted to make a portrait of me as I am. A body of flesh and bones, and intricate
 interplay of organs, bones and, more abstractly, mind.
 The result is my most recent work, a twofold project with the title Body of Work (2019). The first part
 of the project is a series of body parts, exact copies of my own organs, 3D prints based upon medical
 scanning techniques, made of mirroring materials that produce endless reflections of the spectator
 and the presented objects. It plays with the concepts of inside and outside, of the inner and outer, of
 the self and other.
  The second part of the project is a highly innovative series of objects portraying my “creative
 thoughts”. In a series of FMRI scans, made in collaboration with several brain scientists, I mapped
 my brain activity while scientists stimulated me to think about this project and while creating art.
 This activity is translated into sculptures and video, in which I try to decipher my creative mind.
 Looking at my work up to now, I realize that my work is diverse yet consistent. My style and
 aesthetics are wide-ranging, working in mediums including sculpture, video, drawing and painting.
 Nevertheless they share certain characteristics. Not only do I take my personal experiences as a
starting point, I work in an almost scientific way. Data collection, whether based upon my life or
 society, forms the basis of my work. In addition I collaborate with scientists and experts to make
 
optimal use of the data collected. With military experts I composed an overview of military hierarchy,
 with doctors and neuroscientists I have delved into anatomy and my own body. I collaborated with
 NGO’s related to the food industry for Food Chain Project.
 It is the scientific turn that I want to take in the following years - how can I push my own research and
 the results I gather? How can I merge art and science even more in my autonomous work?
attributes.Text:
Itamar Gilboa lives and works in Amsterdam, where his practice moves between art, technology, science, and environmental research. Through meticulous investigation and data-driven methodologies, Gilboa creates immersive sculptural installations that operate at the intersection of poetic reflection and academic inquiry. His work often transforms intimate personal information into statistical narratives, prompting viewers to consider both individual identity and shared human experience.

He received his BFA from the Gerrit Rietveld Academie (2005) and has exhibited internationally in numerous solo and group exhibitions. including at MOCAK Museum of Contemporary Art (Kraków), Ummuseum (South Korea) and Gungpyeong Art Museum Archive (South Korea), the COP26 UN Climate Summit (Glasgow), Jerwood Space (London), Museum Beelden aan Zee (Scheveningen), the Jewish Historical Museum (Amsterdam), and the Tel Aviv Museum of Art (Tel Aviv). Forthcoming exhibitions will take place at the Amsterdam Museum and the Museo Internazionale delle Ceramiche in Faenza. His works are represented in major public and private collections, including the LAM Museum, Ummuseum, AkzoNobel Art Foundation, ING Art Collection, House of Orange-Nassau Royal Collections, DSM Art Collection, Siemens, Rosewood Amsterdam, OLVG Amsterdam, and numerous private collections worldwide.

Balancing the personal with the social has long been a central thread in Gilboa’s practice. While his own biography often acts as a point of departure, he examines his experiences through the behavior, stories, and perspectives of others. Cultural background, national identity, migration, social networks, and personal transformation all serve as lenses through which broader societal issues emerge. By expanding metaphors drawn from his own life, he addresses larger cultural questions, revealing more of himself in the process than initially intended.

After moving to Amsterdam in 2001, Gilboa became acutely aware of the shifts in his daily rhythm, dietary habits, and social environment. This led him to use his own life as material for art-making. Early projects such as I Want to Be Green (2005) and Rijtjeshuizen (2006–2008) examined the migrant experience through video works and sculptures, sharing stories of Israelis living in the Netherlands and Dutch emigrants living in Israel. Both projects were presented at the Joods Historisch Museum in Amsterdam.

His research-based approach continued in Chief of Stuff (2011), a mixed-media installation exploring the power structures of the Israeli military through the symbolic language of loyalty, sacrifice, obedience, and tradition. Drawing from his background as a young soldier in an elite combat unit, Gilboa investigated the distance between who he once was and the forces that shaped that identity. This inquiry expanded into The Chief of Staff (2011), a site-specific installation for the Herzliya Museum of Contemporary Art. Through extensive interviews with military historians and experts, he mapped the hierarchy of Israel’s military command, translating each rank into a series of 161 paintings depicting commanders as fallen angels.

These projects were rooted in personal experience yet positioned Gilboa as a social observer. This shifted significantly with the Food Chain Project, initiated in 2008, where he undertook a deeply personal and meticulous process: recording every item he ate and drank for a full year without looking at the list until the end. In 2013 he began translating this data into thousands of white plaster sculptures modeled from actual food items and installed them as a single supermarket-like environment.

Four years later, he created a new porcelain version of the installation for the LAM Museum, presented on meticulously arranged shelving. Working with this delicate medium pushed his technical limits while reinforcing the conceptual underpinnings of the project. Through the 8,000 food items he consumed in a year, Gilboa opened a conversation about overconsumption, global food inequality, and the everyday choices underpinning larger socio-economic systems. What began as an analysis of personal habits became, in its totality, an unintentional self-portrait — a large-scale reflection of the saying “you are what you eat.”

This realization sparked a deeper investigation into the history and meaning of self-portraiture. Connecting contemporary notions of self-representation — from selfies to psychological research on identity — with centuries-long traditions of introspection, Gilboa sought to create a portrait grounded not in metaphor but in physical reality.

This led to Body of Work (2019), a two-part project. The first consists of exact replicas of his organs, 3D-printed from medical scans and cast in reflective materials that blur the boundaries between viewer and object, inside and outside, self and other. The second translates his own neural activity into sculptural forms. Through a series of fMRI scans conducted with neuroscientists, Gilboa mapped his brain while he conceived and developed the project itself. The resulting works — sculptures and video — visualize the processes behind creative thought.

Across his diverse practice, Gilboa consistently integrates personal experience with scientific inquiry. Data collection serves as both method and metaphor, whether examining military structures, the human body, or global food systems. His collaborations with experts — military analysts, doctors, neuroscientists, and NGOs — deepen the rigor of his investigations. Looking ahead, Gilboa continues to expand the ways in which scientific research can inform and transform artistic practice, seeking new possibilities at the boundary where art and science converge.

Food Chain Project
attributes.Text:
**FOOD CHAIN PROJECT (2013-PRESENT)** 

The Food Chain Project is a pop-up supermarket made entirely of sculptural groceries, representing Gilboa's consumption over 365 days.

Each individual piece of the installation — ranging from a lemon to a carton of milk and from a can of tuna to a hot dog — could be purchased separately during the exhibition. A percentage of profits were then donated to NGO's fighting food issues, thereby creating a food chain. "What I ate turned into art, which, when sold, can again become food," explains Gilboa.

Gilboa meticulously kept track of his daily consumption by keeping a diary of everything he ate and drank for the duration of a year. Some three years later, the results were shown as a sculptural installation, the Food Chain Project. His installation, a traveling pop-up supermarket consisting of more than 8,000 white plaster sculptural groceries, physically represents Gilboa's yearly food consumption.

Thinking about personal consumption habits, Gilboa researched the social implications of individual consumption choices on global food issues. By presenting the 8,000 products he consumed in one year, Gilboa continues to raise awareness and generate wider discussions around global food issues. The installation's thought provoking and inventive approach highlights our overconsumption while hundreds of millions of people around the world still suffer from hunger every single day.

attributes.Title: Body of Work
attributes.Text:
**BODY OF WORK (2019)**

Body of Work is a conceptual series of self-portraits, exploring the relationship between identity and the body.

As a starting point for this project, Gilboa collected data using the most advanced medical imaging technologies available – fMRI, MRI and CT scans. With this medical data, he created an installation of sculptural representations of his own body: a body of flesh and blood, an interplay of organs, bones and, more abstractly, his mind. It’s an “ultimate selfie” of sorts, investigating inner and outer layers of the self, while simultaneously referencing modern medicine and mortality.

[Body of Work](https://www.beeldenaanzee.nl/nl/itamar-gilboa), the presentation of his eponymous project, took place in Museum Beelden aan Zee in June 2019. The installation consisted of photographs, videos and sound installation, and sculptures. Upon entering into an enclosed space, viewers became both spectator and object. Each 3D printed body part had a chrome finish and was placed on its own mirrored pedestal. The result was a maze of different planes and endless reflections. The installation played with the concepts of inside and outside, of the inner and outer, of self and other. 

Although Gilboa makes use of the most advanced techniques available in medical sciences, this project is far more than an anatomical lesson. For Gilboa, the importance of this conceptual artwork is exploration of the self and the meaning that it carries.


The project is generously  supported by Siemens Medical Technology, Stratasys, Anatomage, Scannexus, Tel Aviv University, Rivas Hospitals, Radboud UMC,Outset NL and, Mondriaan Fund.

attributes.Title: ArTies
attributes.Text:
**ArTies (2011)**

This Internet presentation reflects the visible and hidden networks of ties within the Israeli art world from Gilboa's starting point. This work was created specifically for the "Facelook" exhibition at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.

In this presentation you will find the people who exert influence in the Israeli cultural world in the spheres of: painting, sculpture, video-art, curatorship, music, cinema, theater, dance, literature, poetry, design, theory and criticism.

Gilboa approached nine individuals from the Israeli art world, and asked them a question which he had previously asked himself, and to which they were the answer: "Please choose up to nine names of people in the Israeli art world (living or deceased) you are connected to/ are influenced by/ appreciate/ are grateful to."

The same question was then sent to the nine names received from the first nine individuals. In turn, they named nine more people whom Gilboa's then approached with the same question, and so forth. Thus, a kind of exponential sequence evolved in multiples of nine, creating a ramified, living, contemporary network of ties and influences within the local cultural sphere.

attributes.Title: Rijtjeshuizen
attributes.Text:
**RIJTJESHUIZEN (2006-2008)**

"Rijtjeshuizen" portrays a bundle of personal meetings with Dutch citizens who chose to live in Israel. The projection of each meeting in the context of a miniature home, creates the perception of visiting one's private territory, the physical and emotional homes of the interviewees.

Over the course of the interviews, Gilboa examined the complex relationship between a citizen and a place. The observer is repeatedly exposed to the indecision of whether or not to leave the Netherlands and move to Israel. Interviewees acknowledge their difficulties, and their dreams that have been partially realized. It draws the conclusion that this specific decision making process (moving to Israel) is wrapped in an identity dilemma.

In the videos, a diverse collection of identities within the Israeli society reveals itself— a society consisting of veteran and new immigrants from diverse religious and cultural backgrounds, living in a country where issues like borders and self-definition are inextricably bound to one's daily routine.

"Rijtjeshuizen" creates a basis to deal with identity on different levels and leaves the spectator, together with the interviewee, in a space where the very term ‘identity’ remains unsolved and unfinished.

attributes.Title: Nacht Gallery
attributes.Text:
**NACHT GALLERY (2005-2010)**

A collaborative art space where Rietveld Academie students were given the opportunity to present and promote their work. The gallery organized 5 exhibitions and events per year through open-calls and competitions.

attributes.Title: Chief of Stuff
attributes.Text:
**CHIEF OF STUFF (2010)**

In this exhibition, Gilboa dealt with the alienation of one who used to live in complete symbiosis with his homeland –up to the point of wanting to become Chief of Staff– but then moved to a foreign land, outgrew his misconceptions, and still felt homesick.

But homesick for what? A land that has changed? The person he once was?

The endless reproduction of his self-portrait in the image of a military target, combined with the figure of the Japanese Samurai, created the image of the ultimate warrior. The multitude of media and pieces emphasized the irony in which the disillusioned artist, looking upon the boy who dreamed of becoming Chief of STAFF, created a grotesque yet sentimental self-portrait of one who has instead become the Chief of STUFF.

attributes.Title: The Food Waste Effect
attributes.Text:
**THE FOOD WASTE EFFECT (2021)**

Inside a sleek greenhouse, a long, thin dinner table showcases over 500 white plaster sculptures of common food items, resembling a grand feast. However, the installation is inaccessible. With no way to enter, no chairs, and no cutlery, it is moreso a memorial to excess rather than an invitation to dine. 

The sculptures represent the 244 kilograms of food discarded annually by a typical British family. Above the table, an LED display presents data on daily food consumption and waste in the UK, such as: “Today alone, 4.4 million potatoes, 20 million slices of bread and 1.2 million tomatoes will be thrown away in the UK”.*

“The Food Waste Effect'' by Itamar Gilboa not only highlights the progress in food production and distribution over the last century, but also underscores the problems of localized overabundance and waste at the expense of natural resources elsewhere. The installation is based on the premise that how we eat reflects who we are, and the understanding that changing our eating habits can be difficult and politically charged. Gilboa implies that reducing food waste is not solely an individual's responsibility, given the complexity of global food distribution and inequality. Nonetheless, the installation proposes that small changes like appreciating potato skins or reducing waste, can have a significant impact. It urges viewers to make the most of available food by enjoying, sharing, and celebrating it. It encourages focus on taste and quality rather than quantity. It advocates for a deeper connection with food production and consumption.

Food is linked to emotions, class, pride, and tradition. The Food Waste Effect questions society’s current prioritization of quantity over quality, quick and easy food over thoughtful preparation, and the influence of price and availability on wasteful and unhealthy choices. Ultimately, it supports a total reconsideration of our relationship with food and our impact on the planet and its inhabitants.

*data based on findings from The Waste and Resource Action Programme (WRAP).

Exhibited at COP 26 UN Summit for Climate Change in Glasgow, Scotland.

attributes.Title: World of Plenty
attributes.Text:
**WORLD OF PLENTY (2024)**

Ease often comes at an unforeseen price. Humanity is becoming aware that Western patterns of consumption have become – or perhaps always have been – unsustainable. We see that hunger is on the rise in many parts of the world, and we must address its root causes. Waste and overconsumption are among some of the largest issues forcing climate change. The changing climate causes droughts, floods, and extreme weather events, which are exacerbating hunger and malnutrition all around the world. And the reality is, as the years go by, the situation has only gotten worse.

Gilboa’s practice is based on translating intimate and emotional experiences into the often confronting rationality of raw data to relay important insights into broader societal statistics and issues. His installation World of Plenty follows this same pattern: increasing awareness of global problems starting with a private experience. The work began with a personal [hunger experiment](https://www.instagram.com/p/CuizHIooVel/) in the fMRI machine, capturing Gilboa’s own brain activity in reaction to hunger. This monumental sculptural pile includes 25,000 recreations of Gilboa’s brain activity in response to hunger, signifying the number of people who tragically die from hunger-related causes each day.*

World of Plenty spreads awareness, illuminates the influence our actions have on increasing hunger, and makes tangible the problems that afflict our society. In a world where the scale of hunger can be overwhelming, Gilboa emphasizes that every global issue has a personal dimension. Small actions can collectively make a difference and ensuring that no one has to endure the pain and indignity of hunger.

*data based on the United Nations 2022 State of Food Security and Nutrition report.

attributes.Title: Cogito Colorum - Color. Wave. Mind.
attributes.Text:
**COGITO COLORUM - COLOR. WAVE. MIND. (2022)**

In a continued exploration with fMRI, Gilboa delves into the fascinating realm of color perception.

In this series, Gilboa examines his brain's activity while meditating upon the entire spectrum of colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. His overarching questions revolve around understanding the physical effects of these colors on our brain functions and whether it's possible to discern a person's mental state in relation to color.

While fMRI has become a pivotal tool across the fields of neuroscience, psychology, and medicine, Gilboa uniquely extends its application into the realm of art. Each fMRI session centers on a specific color, enabling the isolation and visualization of brain activity clusters within the visual processing regions of the brain. These clusters are then transformed into sculptures. Gilboa's captivating approach converts his internal emotional responses to colors into tangible, external artworks - opening up boundless possibilities for translation.

Collaborating closely with brain scientist Job van den Hurk, Gilboa aspires to forge connections between science, technology, and art, ultimately expanding our collective understanding of the human experience.

In Latin, "Cogito Colorum" translates to "I think of colors," encapsulating the essence of this visionary project.

This endeavor was made possible through the utilization of the Siemens Healthineers scanners at the Scannexus facilities in the Netherlands, providing some of the most advanced and accurate results we humans currently have access to.

attributes.Title: The Chief of Staff
attributes.Text:
**THE CHIEF OF STAFF (2011)**

The one hundred sixty-one paintings comprising this work depict the IDF hierarchy, a social model founded on chain of command, orders, and obligatory obedience.

Gilboa explored the principles of the ideological warrior —loyalty, sacrifice, obedience, belief in tradition and the order of the world— by addressing the symbols of military cliché: the enemy as target; the dead (fallen) solider as an angel (or demon); quantity as a value.

The military structure is an ordered, rational, and formal domain. Each function and rank is represented by attributes of a particular size, shape, material and color, from the chief of staff at the top, to last of the privates at the bottom. The military target element throughout the work expresses the individual, the personal, as a part of the comprehensive group, a part of the whole. The reproduction of the target and its reoccurrence expresses the relation between the individual and their surroundings, the tension between seniority and juniority, and the fracture inherent to the system by its very definition.

Created as part of the ‘Nominator & Denominator’ exhibition at the Herzliya Museum of Contemporary Art.

attributes.Title: Project Stimulus
attributes.Text:
**PROJECT STIMULUS (2023)**

Stichting Project Stimulus is a wide ranging research project, bringing together artistic, scientific, and medical institutions. It investigates the impact of the art exhibition experience on the well-being of hospital staff. The project is led by Stichting Stimulus in collaboration with teams from the OLVG Amsterdam Hospital, the Amsterdam Museum, and the University of Amsterdam.

Project Stimulus wishes to explore and research:

- How can museums and hospitals collaborate to create sustainable working and living environments?
- Can the experience of an art exhibition help to relieve fatigue and induce mental recovery in hospital staff?
- How to measure the impact of the art experiment on one’s well-being?

Museums and cultural institutions increasingly aspire to play an essential role in the well-being of their public. In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) acknowledged the significant role of the arts in promoting health. The effect of the arts and the environment on the individual's well-being are receiving increased attention, yet their interaction has been largely neglected. For this purpose, the Stimulus Project will curate art exhibition environments within hospitals, and measure the effects of these environments on hospital staff. Hospital personnel will be exposed to different artistic interventions. The hospital space is mostly designed for efficiency and is indifferent to the spatial experience. In the art exhibition experience, on the other hand, the synergy of art and its spatial environment plays a central role. With Stichting Stimulus, we research the dialogue between the two. This emphasis on the spatial element of experiencing art distinguishes this project from existing research.

Project Stimulus’ first intervention is taking place right now in the Emergency Department at OLVG West.

Members of the Stimulus Project:
Itamar Gilboa, Obbe Tiddens, Alessandra Laitempergher, Mariska Zwartsenburg and Noa Roei

attributes.Title: I Want To Be Green
attributes.Text:
**I WANT TO BE GREEN (2005)**

This installation deals with the geographical transition and acclimation of young Israelis living in the Netherlands. Gilboa selected a group of sixteen people aged 25-40, that represent a broad range of social layers in Israeli society. Interviews were conducted in English and were filmed over 45-minute sessions.

Subjects were continuously confronted with questions about the duration of their stay in the Netherlands, their habits, identities, relationships, shifting perspectives, legal statuses, passageways between countries, families, and future aspirations. Gilboa collected 15 hours of personal monologue footage that captured each subject’s attitude concerning the above-mentioned topics.

“I Want To Be Green” is a 13'37" installation, where visitors enter into an enclosed dark space and are confronted with images and voices. The voices emerge from projections of the expressionless faces of two local actors, suggesting a dialogue. What at first appears to be a dialogue, is in fact a collage of many short monologues from the original interviewees. Quickly viewers realize that the two actors speak with many different voices, and so they speak for all.

The interviewees experience alienation from the local community. They encounter emotional struggles as a result of separating from their country of birth, cultural isolation and the realization that there is no escaping being a stranger in an adopted country. They are compelled to ask: “Do I really long to assimilate? Do I really want to be green?"
